title: A Choir for the House
premise: Xanthe Dunmore hosts a late-night radio show from a decommissioned chapel in the village of Marrow Fen, taking calls from listeners who, he slowly admits to himself, all died the previous week. The house he shelters his estranged family in is one of the old 'counted houses'—dwellings the parish once tallied for a tithe of souls—and when the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins to ring, the count resumes. Xanthe discovers his broadcasts have been keeping the tally at bay: every voice on air is a soul deferred. To save his daughter and her mother, he must choose between staying invisible forever and giving the count his own name, ending the ledger by becoming its final entry.
about_author: Felix Thackeray is the pen name of a former night-shift radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining transmitters in coastal parishes and swears half his listener mail arrived postmarked after the senders' funerals. He writes in the small hours because, as he puts it, 'the dead keep better hours than editors.'

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. A routine broadcast takes its first wrong turn when a caller describes her own funeral in fond detail. Xanthe keeps talking, keeps the signal clean, and afterward counts the doors of the house twice before sleeping. Beat: dread disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: The Counted Houses
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Researching the chapel's deeds, he finds the 1911 parish ledger listing 'counted houses,' including his own, with a column of names struck through except one. His daughter Wren notices him burning paper and asks nothing, which hurts more. Beat: the past has paperwork.

chapters.title: Caller on Line Two
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. The dead callers grow specific—one recites the layout of Xanthe's kitchen, another hums the hymn from Wren's christening. He realizes they aren't haunting him; they're queuing. Beat: intimacy curdling into surveillance.

chapters.title: Wren Hears It Too
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Twelve-year-old Wren hears the bell while walking home and finds the church tower empty, its beam scorched where a bell once hung. She tells no one, practicing instead how to lie like her father does. Beat: inheritance of silence.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't Cast
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. The bell rings at 3 a.m., audible across the village though it was melted down in 1911. Neighbors gather in the lane, some weeping, some counting aloud. Xanthe pulls his family indoors and bolts the doors. Beat: private secret becomes public event.

chapters.title: Mother Merrow's Tithe
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. In the parish archive he learns of Mother Merrow, who in 1911 promised the village would 'pay its count in full' when the bell rang again. The last entry in her hand is a Dunmore name. Beat: the debt predates him.

chapters.title: Static Sermon
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. On air, a new voice preaches through static about ledgers and light. Callers fall silent when it speaks; only the living can hang up. Xanthe realizes his show isn't entertainment—it's a dam. Beat: purpose revealed, burden doubled.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren counts eleven doors in a six-door house. Each extra door opens onto the same hallway, slightly older, wallpaper peeling further back in time. She marks them with chalk; by morning the chalk is gone. Beat: the house is keeping its own books.

chapters.title: The Man Who Counts Aloud
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. A polite stranger, Mr. Quill, arrives claiming to be an auditor of 'parochial arrears.' He never blinks and always knows the time. He gives Xanthe until the bell's hundredth ring. Beat: bureaucracy as horror.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe's sister Idris arrives, furious he hid the danger, loyal enough to stay anyway. They fight about their father, who vanished in 1989—the same year the bell last rang once. Beat: love expressed as accusation.

chapters.title: The Hundredth Ring
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The bell rings its hundredth toll; every door in the house opens at once. Quill stands in the lane with an open ledger, reading names. One name glows wet and fresh: Dunmore. Beat: deadline made flesh.

chapters.title: Voices for the Void
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe broadcasts continuously, letting the dead speak, buying days. Each caller's story delays the count but erodes him—he sleeps standing, forgets Wren's birthday mid-sentence. Beat: sacrifice mistaken for control.

chapters.title: Idris Opens a Door
chapters.summary: POV Idris. Idris opens the eleventh door deliberately and steps into 1911's hallway, meeting Mother Merrow mid-sermon. Merrow offers her a bargain: a name struck from the ledger for a name added. Beat: temptation wearing family's face.

chapters.title: The Bargain Struck
chapters.summary: POV Idris. Idris offers her own name to spare Wren's. Merrow accepts—but reveals the ledger wants a head of household, not a volunteer. The deal sours into a trap. Beat: loyalty weaponized.

chapters.title: Quill's Audit
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Quill audits the house room by room, finding Wren's chalk marks and Idris's absence. He explains gently: the count was never punishment—it's collection of what was promised. Beat: horror reframed as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Wren's Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren sneaks into the studio and takes calls herself, telling the dead stories about the living until they laugh. The bell falters mid-ring. For one hour, the count forgets itself. Beat: innocence as resistance.

chapters.title: Merrow's Regret
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Through the eleventh door, Xanthe confronts Mother Merrow, who confesses she invented the tithe to save her own daughter in 1911—and failed anyway. She tells him how to end it: give the count a name freely given, not taken. Beat: villain becomes mirror.

chapters.title: The Family Vote
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe confesses everything. Idris demands to take his place; Wren proposes tricking the ledger with a false name. They argue, weep, and finally agree: no one goes alone, and no one lies to the count. Beat: unity forged in terror.

chapters.title: Ninety-Nine Doors
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The house grows a ninety-ninth door. Quill waits in the hall with the ledger open to the final page, which holds one blank line. The bell hangs silent above the tower, waiting to be answered. Beat: stillness before the climax.

chapters.title: A Name Freely Given
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. Xanthe signs the ledger with his own name and walks into the tower as the bell swings. But Wren's voice comes through the studio speakers, broadcasting his name back to him—reminding the count he is already heard, already kept. The ledger splits between two claims. Beat: climax, love against duty.

chapters.title: The Last Toll
chapters.summary: POV Xanthe. The count, unable to reconcile a soul both given and held, closes the ledger unfinished. The bell cracks mid-toll and falls silent forever. Xanthe wakes in the chapel doorway, alive but unable to hear any voice again—living or dead. Beat: survival with a price.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Months later, Wren runs the show, reading letters from listeners who are all, blessedly, alive. Xanthe sits in the booth, mouthing along, content to be counted among the living and nothing more. The final line: 'This is the house, and the house is full.' Beat: quiet resolution.
